note: Which ICS4U activity pages reach which AP Computer Science Principles learning objectives, for the marketing working folder (~/Plantoir Marketing) only — never the shipped ICS4U payload. Same shape and rules as csp-correlation.json (ICS3U): marketing_folder.py appends one embed per code inside each page's existing '## Curriculum connection' block, after the Ontario embeds. Drafted 2026-09-27 by reading every ICS4U page in full — the 74 published activity pages that carry a curriculum block, plus the pages without one (which cannot carry an embed) and the class agendas. 'evidence' quotes the ICS4U page (our words, not the College Board's). An objective is tagged only where the page gives students something to do that the objective describes; AAP-4.A is kept to the pages that meet exponential growth, not every page that compares two polynomial algorithms. Every page with a block that is not tagged is listed under 'dropped', with the reason, so it is not proposed again.

rows.reason: Students write methods on a class, work out what each call returns in the self-check, and give every method a docstring saying what it returns and when it refuses.
rows.evidence: A method is a function defined inside a class

rows.reason: Students keep each record whole in a list of objects, and answer the same membership question with a list and with a dictionary, comparing the two approaches rather than assuming one.
rows.evidence: There is no best container.

rows.reason: Students set the harms of making, running, cooling and discarding computers beside the environmental work computing makes possible, and are told a report giving one side is unfinished.
rows.evidence: Both things are true at once

rows.reason: Students write the tally loop that walks a list item by item, and read a KeyError to decide whether the data or the assumption is wrong before choosing the fix.
rows.evidence: A missing key is a decision, not an accident

rows.reason: Students count steps to see how work grows, meet exponential growth that no faster machine rescues, read that the Halting Problem cannot be decided by any algorithm, and state binary search's need for sorted data.
rows.evidence: as the input grows, how does the work grow?

rows.reason: Students route every change through one method so the rule has one home, and see that the stored representation can change without any caller noticing.
rows.evidence: The internals can change.

rows.reason: Students ask whose data trained an automated rule and who is missing from it, collect less personal data because a file will travel, and weigh a professional code of ethics that includes crediting others' work.
rows.evidence: Whose data trained the rule, and who is missing from it?

rows.reason: Students see that a float is stored in binary with a fixed number of bits, meet the round-off and overflow that follow, and test at the boundaries rather than in the middle.
rows.evidence: Every number your program holds lives in a fixed number of bits.

rows.reason: Students replace three parallel lists with one object per booking, explaining how naming the grouped data removes a whole class of bug, and design the classes from the client's words before coding.
rows.evidence: A class is how you tell the computer they belong together.

rows.reason: Students give each question one owning method so the clash rule exists once, predict what each call returns, and sketch the design on CRC cards first.
rows.evidence: The clash rule now exists once.

rows.reason: Students work out what an unfamiliar program does by running it and following one path, then write down what they learned for the next reader.
rows.evidence: Read like an investigator, not a reader

rows.reason: Students see a correct recursive Fibonacci become unusable through exponential growth, set it beside a loop that returns the same numbers, and read a RecursionError to find the missing base case.
rows.evidence: The fix is a base case, or a loop.

rows.reason: Students write a linear search that traverses the list and a binary search, count how many halvings it needs, and learn that it gives wrong answers on unsorted data.
rows.evidence: Binary search works only on sorted data

rows.reason: Students scope a project with the community partner in the room, split it into owned tasks with dates, roles and stand-ups, and plan milestones through testing and review to handover.
rows.evidence: write a scope document with the partner in the room

rows.reason: Students compare three sorts that produce the same order, see that changing > to >= changes how ties come out, and are told to call the built-in sort in real work.
rows.evidence: Two algorithms with the same Big-O can still be very different to live with

rows.reason: Students build a stack and a queue on an ordinary list with append, pop() and pop(0), and wrap it in a class that offers only the promised operations.
rows.evidence: That is what an abstract data type is

rows.reason: Students write tests of normal, edge and refused inputs against each docstring's promise, and turn every reported bug into a failing test before fixing it.
rows.evidence: Every bug becomes a test, before it is fixed

rows.reason: Students index into a grid row then column, and traverse it with nested loops over every element, one row, one column or a neighbour.
rows.evidence: a grid is a list whose elements are themselves lists

rows.reason: Students use a shared history of commits, branches and merges to work on one program together, resolve a conflict by conversation, and write commit messages as documentation.
rows.evidence: A conflict is not a failure and not an accusation.

rows.reason: Students argue over useful proposals that carry personal data down unreviewed paths, republish others' listings without asking, or rank people in ways nobody intended.
rows.evidence: should somebody make this

rows.reason: Students decide what must be written down so a partner can run and change the program after the team is gone.
rows.evidence: the bus factor

rows.reason: Students examine a model trained on past decisions that applies their patterns as rules, and an automated system that errs less on average while its mistakes land on the same group.
rows.evidence: A model trained on records of past decisions.

rows.reason: Students work out how to credit a teammate, a forum answer, a licensed library or an AI assistant in a comment, and what a licence permits.
rows.evidence: Name the source in a comment

rows.reason: Students write methods on Book and Member, find and fix a missing self and an unassigned attribute, and write functions that loop over a list of books.
rows.evidence: The missing three characters are self.

rows.reason: Students fix a lookup that crashes on a missing item, write a tally that walks a list, and say in one sentence what somebody else's function returns.
rows.evidence: Say in one sentence what this returns

rows.reason: Students count operations to classify growth, see exponential growth overtake any polynomial, count the halvings binary search makes, and review a change that makes sorted data a new requirement.
rows.evidence: exponential growth eventually overtakes any polynomial

rows.reason: Students write PunchCard's methods, predict the output of a method that changes only a local variable, and correct it.
rows.evidence: A method is where a rule lives

rows.reason: Students write recursive procedures, find missing and unreachable base cases, and count how the calls of naive Fibonacci grow exponentially.
rows.evidence: That is exponential growth

rows.reason: Students trace binary search step by step counting comparisons, fix a version that never ends, and write searches that traverse a list.
rows.evidence: which is how binary search proves a value is absent

rows.reason: Students fix a sort that reads past the end, compare > and >= versions that sort the same data differently, and see how > compares strings.
rows.evidence: nothing about the sorted-ness differs between them

rows.reason: Students evaluate append, pop() and pop(0) on a list, build a Stack class on a list, and correct a hold list that serves the wrong person.
rows.evidence: One list, two completely different promises

rows.reason: Students invent a sorting rule with cards, write it as numbered steps another group can follow, then compare every group's rule on the same decks.
rows.evidence: Writing an algorithm is mostly the work of finding the steps you did not know you were taking.

rows.reason: Students run a review protocol that keeps the conversation about the code, and find the input that makes a planted list-removal bug appear.
rows.evidence: It is what keeps a review about the code and not about the person

rows.reason: Students describe what an inherited program does, modify its overdue rule on request, and check the change with loans at exactly 11 and 14 days.
rows.evidence: write down what it does

rows.reason: Students cause and resolve a merge conflict in a shared repository, combining two wanted changes by agreement rather than deleting one.
rows.evidence: hands it back to the humans

rows.reason: Students run two programs that give the same answer to the same question and explain why one takes far longer.
rows.evidence: Same input, same output, same answer, every time.

rows.reason: Students build a tally from two parallel lists, remove an item with list.remove, and watch the lists fall out of step.
rows.evidence: The two lists are joined only by a convention that lives in the programmer's head

rows.reason: Students write methods for two collaborating classes and import them from their own module into a separate program, so the classes can be reused.
rows.evidence: the classes can be reused

rows.reason: Students write Stack and Queue classes whose methods hide an ordinary list behind a fixed set of operations.
rows.evidence: Both classes store their items in an ordinary Python list.

rows.reason: Students traverse a list of volunteer objects to find one, total the hours and find the maximum, reusing the search inside the remove procedure.
rows.evidence: is the pattern everything else is built on

rows.reason: Students count binary search's comparisons at growing sizes, check it agrees with linear search before timing it, and break its sorted-data precondition on purpose.
rows.evidence: A fast wrong answer is not a result

rows.reason: Students set their insertion sort beside Python's built-in sort, which they are told to use in real work, and see how > compares strings by character code.
rows.evidence: Sorting names is sorting.

rows.reason: Students write a program that turns a sheet of donation lines into totals, the most-donated item and a shortage list, and handle quantities that arrive as text.
rows.evidence: Everything arrives from the file as text.

rows.reason: Students write a Volunteer class with methods, and deliberately store no last names, birthdates or addresses because data not kept cannot leak.
rows.evidence: Deciding what not to store is a design decision

rows.reason: Students agree to name every borrowed or generated piece of code in a comment or commit message, and to review the code, never the coder.
rows.evidence: Credit is not optional.

rows.reason: Students write comments, commit messages and handover notes for a reader who cannot see inside their head.
rows.evidence: Write for the next person, who might be you

rows.reason: Students are examined on integer division and remainders, on where a machine's number representation runs out, and on cutting a long routine into subprograms.
rows.evidence: Integer division and remainders

rows.reason: Students prove a faster program still correct with tests, boundary cases included, run on both versions.
rows.evidence: A faster wrong answer is worthless.

rows.reason: Students report on an emerging technology's effects on people: who gains, who loses, and who is affected differently.
rows.evidence: who gains, who loses

rows.reason: Students watch their community partner use the software unaided, and hand over a written guide, known limits and change notes.
rows.evidence: you keep your hands off the keyboard

rows.reason: Students describe an inherited program, pin its current behaviour with tests, reproduce a reported bug with a failing test and fix it.
rows.evidence: Characterise it with tests, before you change a line.

rows.reason: Students ask the person who deals with a real thing what they need to know, design a class from their answers, and document every method.
rows.evidence: Ask the person who deals with it what they need to know

rows.reason: Students build software for a community partner as a team with roles, milestones, reviews and testing, and collect no personal data they do not need.
rows.evidence: Collect nothing you do not need.

rows.reason: Students solve one problem with three containers that must give the same answers, checked on one shared test input with awkward cases.
rows.evidence: One problem. Three solutions. One defensible answer.

rows.reason: Students find bugs by shrinking the program and printing values, and settle a stalled team disagreement with a protocol.
rows.evidence: The gap between what you believe and what prints is where bugs live.

rows.page: Tutorials/Reading a Traceback in Someone Else's Code
rows.reason: Students read a long traceback to find what went wrong and the lowest frame they can change.
rows.evidence: Read the bottom, then find your code

rows.reason: Students use git and a shared hosted repository to work on the same files, and write commit messages that explain why.
rows.evidence: Commit messages are documentation with a deadline

rows.reason: Students run stand-ups, rotate roles, review with prepared sentences, and settle disagreements with an agreed protocol.
rows.evidence: Design disagreements are normal, and they are a sign the team is thinking.

rows.reason: Students write docstrings as contracts, and give classes, variables and settings meaningful names.
rows.evidence: The docstring is a promise

rows.reason: Students choose ordinary and boundary inputs with expected results, watch a test fail, then fix the code it caught.
rows.evidence: Watch every new test fail at least once.

rows.reason: Students diagnose a traceback and decide which frame's code is actually at fault.
rows.evidence: The crash site is not the crime scene

rows.reason: Students predict what a variable holds after assignments and an append when three names refer to one list.
rows.evidence: three names, one object

rows.reason: Students review a change from linear to binary search that looks equivalent but gives a different answer on unsorted data.
rows.evidence: Fast and wrong is worse than slow and right

rows.reason: Students find an off-by-one bound and a shared default list by reading, and correct each.
rows.evidence: The fix is one character of arithmetic

rows.reason: Students trace a recursive procedure call by call to determine what it returns.
rows.evidence: One row per call, not per pass.

rows.reason: Students compare what append, a key lookup, pop(0) and pop() do to a collection.
rows.evidence: Only one removes from the front, and pays for it

dropped.why: The discussion is about who carries the cost of maintaining software over time; no CSP learning objective covers maintenance, and its one line about naming a rate is not enough to claim documentation or abstraction.
A private reflective log of the student's own work; CSP has no objective on self-reflection, and recording a development process is not developing a program with one.
A reflection on the student's own growth, team and career pathways; no CSP learning objective covers self-assessment or careers.
A self-review routine against a task's criteria; CSP has no objective on assessing one's own work.
Teaches citing one's own journal as evidence of growth; no CSP learning objective covers it.
Describes the rhythm of a class period; it asks students to do nothing a CSP learning objective describes.
Separating what a news story claims from what is known is media literacy; the page names who benefits but never asks students to weigh a harm against a benefit, so IOC-1.A is not reached.

Times a linear and a binary search; AAP-4.A asks about reasonable versus unreasonable time, which two polynomial searches never reach, and CSN-2.A's time comparisons concern parallel and distributed solutions.
